clinician.trajectory_summary: A 13-year-old girl presented with a progressive neurological syndrome that began at age 7 with headaches accompanied by right-sided weakness (power 4/5, reduced sensation, brisk reflexes, and minimal facial asymmetry). One year after initial presentation, she developed new-onset complex-partial seizures characterized by mumbling, blank stare, drowsiness, and post-ictal confusion. She was initiated on sodium valproate 200 mg twice daily for seizure management. Brain imaging performed at one year after initial presentation revealed left cerebral hemisphere universal atrophy with ventricular enlargement, ipsilateral calvarial thickening, hyperpneumatization of the left frontal sinus, and a left-sided infarct. These imaging findings are pathognomonic for Dyke-Davidoff-Masson syndrome, a condition characterized by cerebral hemiatrophy with ipsilateral skull thickening and hyperostosis, typically resulting from early cerebral injury.
